records.author: RGS1811
records.storyText:
The linked repo is 100% vibe coded, but it was built on a handful of principles:

- Most tax software derives trust from the party who maintains it (e.g. Intuit, the IRS, etc.)

- Vibe coded software lacks this trustworthiness.

- Therefore any formalization should build in verifiability and mechanisms that make it possible for users/maintainers to trace claims/interpretations back to authoritative source documents.

It's very much a back-burner passive project right now (do not use this for anything real!), but I feel strongly that something like this ought to exist for the public good. I built it to get a sense of what the shape of what such a thing might be.

records.author: polyglotfacto
records.storyText:
Hello HN,

I've been working on a new Web engine, build around two ideas:

- use formal methods from day one. - make it modular.

The modularity is orientated towards the following goals:

- enabling shipping anywhere, including on IOS in the EU as per Apple’s guidelines. - only write code for stuff the OS or application platform cannot do for you: keep binary size to a minimum and achieve native performance. - developer choice: bring what you want, and only build what you need.

For example you can choose a JS engine like v8 or Boa, or just bring your own. The entire graphics pipeline consists of components whose implementation can be swapped-out, with currently a relatively fast path on Mac integrating with Core Animation and a slower cross platform path.

Project is at https://github.com/gterzian/formal-web

Intro essay at: https://medium.com/@polyglot_factotum/how-i-am-building-a-we...

records.title: Show HN: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code
records.author: aray07
records.storyText:
Hey HN,

I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production.

Demo: https://youtu.be/47phxkdh6f0

Example: We tested Opslane on Lago (open-source billing) and found a bug where customers get double charged. Opslane made Stripe take the money and then return a 500. Lago marked the payment failed. A retry from the dashboard charged the customer again. https://github.com/getlago/lago-api/issues/6903

Why I built this

I used to work on reliability at Robinhood. We used to run chaos testing in our staging environments: inject faults in various parts of the system and see what breaks. We found issues like Kafka or Redis being unavailable for a few seconds could take the whole app down.

But that kind of testing was expensive. It needed a well maintained staging environment. Engineers needed to know what to test. Most teams never actually did it.

Over the last year, coding agents have gone writing some of my code to almost all my code now. Teams are shipping way more code than they were 6 months ago.

Code review tools read the diff, but a lot of reliability bugs aren't in the diff. They're in how your code behaves when Stripe, Redis or the network misbehaves. And e2e tests usually mock those services out and test the happy path.

Agents have made this type of testing a lot cheaper. And we will see more of this (kinda like security scanning / testing)

How it works

A full copy of your app per PR: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3.

Working copies of your third-party dependencies: Stripe, Slack, Gmail and more. Traffic goes through our proxy, which lets us inject failures.

The agent picks what to test: It reads every PR and writes down invariants that need to hold (for e.g. a customer should never be charged twice). It then injects faults likely to break the invariants.

Bugs we've found

We ran Opslane on some popular open-source apps and here are some of the bugs we have found:

1/ Twenty: deleting a workspace while Stripe is failing locks everyone out, and billing keeps going. Twenty merged a fix. (https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/28043)

2/ Dub: a restart in the middle of a payout paid a partner $240 for $120 owed. (https://github.com/dubinc/dub.link/issues/4707)

Full list: opslane.com/open-source

Opslane is pretty early - we have a couple of early customers. We have found bugs in their system that their other code review tools missed.

Would love to get feedback from folks and how they are seeing the reliability of their systems evolve over time with agents.

records.title: Show HN: OpenTaxRate – open-source US sales tax rates by street address
records.author: winxton
records.storyText:
I built this because I tried many sales tax APIs and the problems were: a) the rates were a black box with no source attached b) lookups resolved by ZIP code.

ZIP codes are postal routes, not tax jurisdictions. Stripe's Tax team wrote a good post on this [1]: two houses in Drexel, MO share a city, a ZIP, and nearly a house number, but sit in different counties with different rates. If your lookup key is the ZIP, you are wrong on those addresses, even when the rate table is accurate.

OpenTaxRate resolves the street address instead: - SST member states (24): the quarterly rate + boundary files, street ranges and ZIP+4, not just the rate tables - Non-SST states: a custom adapter for each state, using its DOR's own published tables and boundary files (TX Comptroller, FL DR-15DSS, ALDOR, IDOR, NY Pub 718, California via CDTFA's lookup, etc) - Census TIGER for geometry

I tried with multiple open source geocoders you can self-host: Nominatim, Photon and Pelias, as well as proprietary ones (HERE, Geocodio, Mapbox, Google). Proprietary ones have higher accuracy, ~99.3% correct vs. 97.1% with just open source.

For comparison: Avalara AvaTax 99.6%, TaxJar 98.2%. Public benchmark set are in the repo and at opentaxrate.com/benchmarks.

Rates are just one part of sales tax, but also there's a ton of work in maintaining it as rules change. It doesn't handle exemptions, holidays, and caps.

It returns the rate, plus the state's own location and jurisdiction codes for the address, resolved to the address, with its official source attached. MIT licensed, you can self-host with Postgres + PostGIS.

[1]: https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-jurisdiction-resolut...

records.title: Show HN: Potential conversation partners in Bluesky using agentic search
records.author: wolecki
records.storyText:
What if instead of talking to AI, we could find human counterparts currently sharing the same interest to talk to? Some whales kind of do that by singing across the ocean.

This inspired a thought process for a conceptual social network - whalesong - where an idea, thought or a conversationally valuable statement could be matched on.

In contrast with the wide-broadcast social network visibility (restricted on groups or connections), I’d love to explore the idea of context-based networking.

This experiment is showcasing the technical feasibility and potential value in whalesong.

The goal: uncover conversational counterparts among Bluesky posts using an agentic search algorithm.

The setup: a one-week window of bluesky posts with some filtering (e.g. mostly text, no promotions or reposts/comments), indexed in a postgres database. A curated seed set - an agentic process defines a conversation-seeking cohort by creating some heuristic queries, iterating and validating it on retrieved data and resulting in a non-exhaustive set of high-quality data points. Counterpart retrieval - for a seed conversation-seeking post, an agentic process generates search queries, runs them against the database and retrieves potential matches. It reviews retrievals and iterates on improving or expanding the search.

Out of several configurations, the best performing agentic setup (bespoke mini-harness with Gemini Argon - low) managed to find meaningful matches to 79% of a sample set of 100 seeds. This setup consumed on average 42K input tokens on each match search, of which 56.8% were cached, output token count was negligible.

So this experiment made it clearer to me that technology is not the blocker for a “whalesong” experience. This leads me to further investigate the experience itself. Would love to hear from you folks about experiences in getting in touch with a complete stranger on the web because both of you asked the same question or had a similar problem to solve. What made you connect? Where did it happen? Did finding similarity make connecting easy?

records.title: Show HN: MealWords – Show waiters what you can't eat, in their language
records.author: LewisOrton
records.storyText:
Last month I went to Indonesia, and was eating at a local place with friends who did not eat raw fish&green onions. We tried ChatGPT (of course) it worked, except it wasnt a smooth experience: taking too long, and difficult for the staff to provide proper feedback quickly.

Then I realized I only needed to tell the waiter what we won't eat, and ask for recommendations, that's all. So I made MealWords (recommend to try on your phone):

1. You pick allergies, dietary and preferences in your language (peanuts, no cilantro, not spicy etc) and it shows the card in the staff's language.

2. The waiter taps anything they can't do on the card, or just confirms. You read the answer in your own language.

On translations: nothing is machine-translated (well, llm-assisted for research but not mechanical translations). For allergens&terms I used all official guidance I could find (FDA, EFSA, Japan etc all official governments and local public health orgs) to make sure I used not only accurate but also understandable terms. Then I worked with native speakers (aka my friends all over the world) to proofread it as plain kitchen language, NOT medical wording (if you speak one of the languages and something feels odd, I'd really like to know!) Also, wordings were carefully chosen to meet local culture (for example if the target language is Chinese, there are extra explanations about peanut allergy when chosen, and what local sauces should be avoided in Chinese, where the general are not familiar with the concept enough compared to other places like Japan)

Technical bits: the website is static, no account, card and choices stay in the browser (page analytics etc are described on the privacy page as they are but no privacy is collected)

records.title: Show HN: Wavefunction – a minimal, open-source desktop coding agent for Mac
records.author: spstoyanov
records.storyText:
During the dark ages of AI, when Opus 5 was incomprehensible and Codex Ultra was burning all tokens within a day, I decided to give open-source agents and models a try.

What I saw was that a lot of the tools I tried were terminal-first, and desktop apps were less common.

Additionally, I felt that lately a lot of the agents apps are slowly trying to become “superapps”. They keep adding more and more features that imo are not always useful and make the UI quite heavy and complex.

This motivated me to build Wavefunction: A minimal, open-source app desktop app that focuses on the coding experience and tries to reduce unnecessary features.

It doesn’t have a built in browser and its computer use functionality works in a VM.

I built it on top of langgraph and it’s packaged as a tauri desktop app.

Currently, It works with Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter, Anthropic API key, Google AI Studio API key, and you can log in with your ChatGPT account or use a local model with Ollama.

It also has 70+ connectors.

Last, but not least, you can also require ZDR-only models from the providers.

  If you try it out I would love to hear your feedback! Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Google translate replacement for language learners
records.author: musabilhan
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Musab and I'm building Manalect. Find TL;DR at the end.

Most language apps fall short for me in two ways:

1. They’re not personalized enough. I get taught things I don’t care about, things that are too hard for me, and things I already know. 2. They don’t teach that well. I keep seeing question types where my brain does almost no work to figure out the answer, therefore learn nothing.

I think the biggest reason they're not personalized enough is that they don't have a detailed enough representation of a language. Most apps have efficient review scheduling for the words you learn. But if you make the mistake of using "play" instead of "played" they're not able to identify that as a component that should have its own schedule for review. And if you don't track that, it essentially depends on luck whether a person reviews that information before forgetting it again.

Essentially language isn't just made up of words, but also different forms, conjugations, phrases, grammar, and a lot more components.

But mapping out the basic units in full detail isn't enough. It's also very important to know how those basic units relate to each other. Because of course some units share a lot in common, and their relationships form another unit that needs to be tracked.

Take Spanish: “el gato negro” (the black cat) but “la casa negra” (the black house). “negro” becomes “negra” because “casa” is a feminine word. That rule isn’t part of any one word. It links the noun, its article and the adjective, and it shows up in almost every sentence. So it needs its own review schedule too. And it relies on a person knowing those things that make it up to be able to build that block.

That was briefly about how I'm working on solving the first failure mode. Second is simpler but also very interesting. We know that for you to learn something, you need to experience difficulty. This is called desirable difficulty.

For this reason, some question types, like multiple choice, are known to be inefficient. But that's not fully true. The reason multiple-choice questions can be inefficient is that usually the alternative options are so much more different from the correct one that it is very easy to guess which one is the right one. However, if you make a simple change where you make it so the alternatives are a lot closer to the correct answer, the person has to put more effort into recalling the correct option. In research, this is known as competitive distractors.

And of course, desirable difficulty is not the same for everyone. This is quite simple to imagine. Even games allow you to change the difficulty, and the difficulty that is most efficient for learning doesn't necessarily have to be the difficulty a person can sustain for the long term. So it's also very personal.

I had written a lot more about how it works in detail, but due to the allowed length for this post, I'll get to how specifically the app works on an application level. Please let me know if you have any questions. I'm very passionate about this, and I would love to talk more.

How it works:

1. Translate sentences, define words, chat with AI, or import an article or a song 2. The content gets broken into granular components, not just words but grammar and more complex building blocks) and saved for you 3. You study them as short tests in real sentences 4. Stuff you already know gets skipped, and new stuff builds on what you know

You can try it at manalect.com, no sign-up needed. Swedish, German, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Polish or English. It's free with a daily limit.

It's at an early stage, and there might be bugs, but I'd love to hear from you about them so that I can fix them right away.

I'd also love to hear your thoughts, and how you learn languages in general. I'll be around all day to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: Fast, Zero Allocation, AOT Safe, Compile-Time Safe .NET Template Engine
records.author: ggende
records.storyText:
I built a text templating engine, that I've named Lissic, as part of a personal website project I'm working on. It fits a niche that I don't think anything else in the .NET ecosystem fills. I prefer to keep code out the template itself (separation of concerns, view vs model, and all that). I also wanted to build something simple enough that I could imagine low/medium-tech UI dev working with it, but it still needs to build things in a modular way, support loops, support conditional/branching views, and have the ability to format/filter values inserted into the text.

I've improved Lissic to the point that I think it's worth sharing with the community. A quick overview of the features:

- Renders near twice as fast as the fastest major .NET templating engine (see below) - Zero allocation with default settings, when rendering to a buffer (e.g. to HttpResponse.BodyWriter) - 100% AOT compatible without any restrictions (no use of Reflection or dynamic) - Simple but powerful tagging system that keeps a clear division between layout and logic - Compile-time safety with source-generated Data Transfer Objects that automatically adjust to each template's text - Define templates directly in code with text or import them from template files - Transformation pipeline that allows using Formatters to modify how values are converted to text and Filters to modify text before insertion - Hot reload for file-based templates in debug mode - Thorough AI-friendly documentation (I gave only the documentation to QWEN3.8-27B, and it was able to make a simple task-management web app)

A full BenchmarkDotNet chart is in the GitHub README, but here's a quick rendering comparison:

Lissic (RenderToString) - 8.814 us / 18072 B

Lissic (RenderToBuffer) - 8.482 us / 0 B

Fluid - 15.593 us / 37128 B

Fluid (SourceGenerated) - 24.045 us / 49128 B

Scriban - 70.985 us / 144025 B

Handlebars - 21.944 us / 122176 B

It uses tags that look similar to many other templating engines. It has tag types to insert direct values ("variables"), other templates ("parts"), and lists of templates ("loops"). It also has branching logic that works a lot like a switch statement (i.e. define keys, and the text and/or code that goes with each key).

Very simple example:

---------------------------------------------

  [TemplateText("Hello {{ name <upper> }}!")]
  public partial class LissicExample {}
  
  // Automatically transforms the partial class into a DTO, with a property for each tag
  LissicExample myTemplate = new() { name = "John" };
  
  // LissicProcessor retrieved from Dependency Injection
  lissicProcessor.RenderToBuffer(myTemplate, HttpResponse.BodyWriter);
  
  // Writes "Hello JOHN!" to the HTTP response body
---------------------------------------------

The main tradeoff at this time is that all templates are defined at startup (other than the debugging-only hot reload option), so it's not really a general purpose user-provided template engine. This leaves it comparable to libraries like Fluid or Scriban in some ways, but comparable to Razor Pages in others. It works really well for my purpose and preferences though.

I'd appreciate any feedback anyone has. I'd like to keeping building this for the long haul. If nothing else, I'll be updating it for work in my own project.

In particular, I'd like to support using literal text in loop tags, but that doesn't work cleanly with my current auto-generated DTO setup. I've considered auto-generating DTOs with predictable names (and providing a name override option via attributes). I've also considered supporting duck-typing for those, which would essentially be a new feature set, which is maybe useful or maybe over complicating it? I'd appreciate thoughts on this in particular. :)

Shout out to Andrew Lock and his Creating a Source Generator series!

The code is at https://github.com/gendeg/Lissic, and it's on NuGet (package name: Lissic)

records.title: Show HN: Vu – a new programming language designed for AI. Rust speeds, Py syntax
records.author: vu0tran
records.storyText:
hi everyone! I wanted to share what I've been working on these past 6~ years.

TL;DR: Rust is great, but somewhere along the way, I learned that I was too dumb to read and write Rust. As I worked on larger and larger Rust projects, I also became frustrated with the developer experience of working in Rust (slow compile time), so I wanted a better way.

Vu's language changed a bit over time but the core principles remained the same:

1. It should be easy to read and write 2. It should be memory safe 3. It should be fast to run 4. It should be fast to compile

Here's how I approached each:

1. Vu is syntactically very close to Python. The ownership rules are the ones Rust has, but I personally find it a lot easier to parse and understand. I've tested this with various LLMs and found it can read and write Vu out the box because of the similarity to Python.

2. Vu uses the same principles of Rust. Every value has one owner, borrows can't escape or outlive what they borrow, and nothing changes while it's borrowed.

3. Vu compiles down to C at the end of the day, so everything runs approximately at C speeds.

4. vuc check on the compiler’s own source (about 21,500 lines of Vu), takes about 0.4~ s. This check covers parsing, type and borrow checking. cargo check on a Rust project that size usually takes several seconds from scratch. Then there are other opinionated language decisions. Vu has no macros, Vu's borrow checker is lighter weight than Rust's with simpler interfaces and generics.

However, in the past few years, as Vu's language evolved and AI began to take over, I expanded Vu's principles to include a couple additional principles:

5. It should be secure 6. It should be efficient for LLMs to write

5. I want to pen test Vu in public. In https://github.com/vu0tran/vu/tree/main/tests, you'll see a battery of tests where I'm trying to basically pwn Vu. There are explicit language decisions in there as well that tries to prevent a host of security flaws that exist in other languages, e.g, integer overflow stops the program instead of quietly wrapping around.

6. The syntax of Vu is designed to be tokenizer efficient. In addition, when Vu checks throws errors, the errors are designed to be token efficient and written in a way that guides LLMs to more easily fix bugs, reducing turns overall.

So, in summary, Vu is still experimental. The compiler is 21,500 lines of Vu and compiles itself. The standard library also has TLS, HTTP/2, WebSockets and a PostgreSQL client, all tested against Python’s implementations and hostile input. I think most of the pieces are there. It does also compile down also to WebAssembly so you can play around w/ the checker on the website!

Feel free to try to break it!

What's next: 1. Figure out how to get Vu to perform faster than Rust 2. Rewrite some OSS libraries in Vu to further prove the language

records.title: Show HN: LayerShop – a love child of ComfyUI and PhotoCraft
records.author: SlavomirDurej
records.storyText:
You might have seen PhotoCraft, an open-source Photoshop-style editor. It's great, but it was missing one important ingredient: generative AI. LayerShop fills that gap, and unlike Photoshop, it can run the models locally on your own GPU, for free.

Here are the AI features you get with LayerShop:

- a guided ComfyUI install (the engine)

- guided download and setup of local models, including the latest ones like MOSS Image, Ming, Ernie, FLUX.3 Klein, Z-Image, Krea 2 and Ideogram 4

- support for the latest cloud (paid) models like GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare, FLUX 3, Grok Imagine 2 and Nano Banana Pro

It supports text to image, image to image, inpainting and outpainting, named image references, targeted or whole-image edits, style transfer, photo restoration, relighting and more.

All of that in a familiar Photoshop-style UI, on layers with transparency, blend modes and masks.

Every generated layer remembers which model, prompt and settings made it. You can still tweak the advanced settings if you like: number of steps, seed, CFG scale, LoRA strength and more.

It's a first preview: Windows only, NVIDIA for local models, and not code-signed yet. 3-minute demo: https://youtu.be/dCBiipZ03dA

records.title: Show HN: Seqora – Desktop DB Workbench for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite
records.author: duoro
records.storyText:
I built Seqora as a solo developer because I was tired of DBeaver and TablePlus, the tools I was using. None of them felt like modern tooling. DBeaver is mature, but it lacks customization and it’s slow. TablePlus puts too many limits on its free tier, like only allowing two tabs open at a time. What I wanted to do differently in Seqora was to let me visualize different objects, like indexes, partitions, etc. Another thing I found most tools lacked was a way to figure out what’s slowing down a complex query, so I built a visual EXPLAIN that shows where the time goes. I put the main focus on those two.

The next thing was being able to work on a connection visually using diagrams, so I can see how things are connected and make changes by drag and drop. Once everything is done, I can review all the SQL that will run.

I made sure the things you need for a daily driver are free, so there’s no limit on the number of queries, connections or tabs. The deep-dive parts, the object views, visual EXPLAIN and schema diagrams, are in Pro. Pro is currently $5.99/month or $49/year. It’s pre-1.0, currently at 0.4.6. It supports macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows, and Linux is coming soon.

It’s built with Tauri, Rust and Svelte. Most of the code was written with Claude Code and ChatGPT. I made the decisions and did the reviewing and testing.

I’d love it if you tried it and told me what you don’t like so I can improve it, and also what you hate about your current workbench.

records.title: Show HN: Universal Blindspot Detector (AI meta-analysis)
records.author: mmazing
records.storyText:
This is a rough "blindspot detector" for AI conversations.

Basically, the tool reframes conversations and tries to find the smallest moves the user COULD have made to have surfaced unknown assumptions for whatever problem they were solving.

The goal is to show the value of using AI as a reflective surface to search for "unknown unknowns" or "things YOU didn't know you needed to know".

-------------------------

The basic premise is this:

For any given AI conversation, the quality of the output (for the specified goal) depends on the context from which decisions can be made.

You can learn to surface assumptions (the AI's AND your own) and get better output from informed decisions. Best of all, when operating in this way, you have to actively engage the problem and strategy to accomplish this, so you don't lose understanding or creative agency.

When you iterate during problem definition or strategy planning, it's cheaper and more efficient, too.

For example:

[# of Planning Phase Iterations] x 1,000 tokens [# of Strategy Phase Iterations] x 3,000 tokens [# of Execution Output Phase Iterations] x 5,000,000 tokens

Usually when we are solving problems with this method, we one-shot the output even with local models like Qwen 3.6/3.8, spending FAR less time in the expensive execution phase.

---------------------------

Anyway, please have a look! Totally free, no signup, you just need to export conversations in specific formats and upload them.

This was made by myself and a few interns in a barn while doing indie game development ... and costs us money, so please don't abuse it. <3

records.author: taychen
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I've had this project idea for years now and finally got some time to work on it while I'm in between jobs.

The main idea is during the incident, users would interact with the slack bot which helps facilitate and gather context. After the incident, the web app has everything to run the postmortem.

The "Try the demo" button creates a temporary workspace with some demo data to play around with.

Would appreciate any feedback! :)

records.storyText:
Knowledge hits you from everywhere - papers, lectures, podcasts, chats - and most of it is gone by Friday, unless you give it a home.

MindForger - thinking notebook - is not intuitive as I build it mostly for myself, but my wife :) had a nice idea to explain what MindForger is about without a wall of text with a comic! It follows one knowledge junkie from the chaos of browser tabs and sticky notes, through typed notes, outlines, notebooks and shelves, Kanban and the Eisenhower matrix, private AI and finding what he wrote weeks ago, all the way to a thinking notebook that is private, free and his.

Enjoy!

records.title: Show HN: X402 integrations for an AI-agent data API, checked in a clean room
records.author: jgmale123
records.storyText: I run Blockchain IQ. We sell some crypto data to software agents per request over x402 (HTTP 402, USDC on Base, no account or API key). In October we paid for integrations: 22 were submitted and we checked each one by matching its on-chain payment to our purchase log and running it in a clean temporary folder with a throwaway wallet. Twenty passed; the post lists all of them with the exact commits we ran. To try the API: `curl -i https://www.blockchainiq.co/api/x402/v1/brief` returns the 402 with the price ($0.01), and a wallet's first call is free. Questions about how we checked the code or what failed are welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Promptuaria – GitHub for specs
records.author: tolarianwiz
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm seeing more and more people sharing software specs instead of code, and I think this will become increasingly common as coding agents get better at one-shotting entire apps from a single prompt.

So I put together Promptuaria over a few days. It's a small platform where you can publish, version, and fork software specs, and link GitHub implementations to the exact spec versions they were built from so you can confront them.

Specs are Git-versioned under the hood, with immutable published versions.

It's an early side project, but I'm curious to know if others see specs becoming something we share and reuse, pretty much like code.

Would love to hear what you think!
